s: Classifications based on race and national origin are inherently suspect, as are state classifications based on alienage (Graham v. Richardson, 1971).
There are exceptions for "political functions" such as police officers and teachers (Cabell v. Chavez-Salido).
Federal alienage rules get deference because of the immigration power.
The government must prove the classification is narrowly tailored to a compelling interest.
Narrow tailoring requires necessity, serious consideration of race-neutral alternatives, a limited scope, and a logical end point.
The tier is often described as "strict in theory, fatal in fact," though Grutter and Korematsu (later repudiated in Trump v. Hawaii) are exceptions.
Dred Scott (1857) denied citizenship to Black Americans.
Strauder v. West Virginia (1880) struck down the exclusion of Black men from juries.
Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) upheld "separate but equal."
Brown v. Board of Education (1954) overruled Plessy in public education: "separate educational facilities are inherently unequal."
Brown II (1955) ordered desegregation "with all deliberate speed."
Loving v. Virginia (1967) struck down interracial-marriage bans.
Equal application to both races does not save a racial classification.
